claim: The centromere is the unique chromosomal locus that forms the kinetochore, which interacts with spindle microtubules and directs segregation of replicated chromosomes to daughter cells.
source: The centromere is the unique chromosomal locus that forms the kinetochore, which interacts with spindle microtubules and directs segregation of replicated chromosomes to daughter cells (McKinley and Cheeseman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKinley and Cheeseman, 2016

claim: Human centromeres assemble on a subset of large blocks (many Mbps) of highly repeated (171 bp) α-satellite arrays found on all chromosomes.
source: Human centromeres assemble on a subset of large blocks (many Mbps) of highly repeated (171 bp) α-satellite arrays found on all chromosomes.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about human centromere structure

claim: Repetitive arrays and the flanking heterochromatin (together the Centromere Proximal Regions or CPRs) play critical roles in the integrity of mitotic and meiotic inheritance.
source: These repetitive arrays and the flanking heterochromatin (together the Centromere Proximal Regions or CPRs) play critical roles in the integrity of mitotic and meiotic inheritance (Janssen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janssen et al., 2018

claim: Chromosome instability, including loss and gain of chromosomes, plays large and complex roles in aging, cancer, and human embryonic survival.
source: In somatic tissues, chromosome instability, including loss and gain of chromosomes, plays large and complex roles in aging, cancer (Naylor and van Deursen, 2016), and human embryonic survival (McCoy, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Naylor and van Deursen, 2016 and McCoy, 2017

claim: Sequence variation in CPRs can affect meiotic pairing.
source: Sequence variation in CPRs can affect meiotic pairing (Dernburg et al., 1996; Karpen et al., 1996), kinetochore formation (Rosin and Mellone, 2017) and nonrandom segregation (Karpen et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dernburg et al., 1996 and Karpen et al., 1996

claim: Sequence variation in CPRs can affect kinetochore formation.
source: Sequence variation in CPRs can affect meiotic pairing (Dernburg et al., 1996; Karpen et al., 1996), kinetochore formation (Rosin and Mellone, 2017) and nonrandom segregation (Karpen et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosin and Mellone, 2017

claim: Sequence variation in CPRs can affect nonrandom segregation.
source: Sequence variation in CPRs can affect meiotic pairing (Dernburg et al., 1996; Karpen et al., 1996), kinetochore formation (Rosin and Mellone, 2017) and nonrandom segregation (Karpen et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karpen et al., 1996

claim: A large component of genetic disease stems from aneuploidies arising during meiosis.
source: A large component of genetic disease stems from aneuploidies arising during meiosis (Nagaoka et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nagaoka et al., 2012

claim: The unique asymmetry of transmission in female meiosis, where only one parental chromosome is transmitted, presents an opportunity for the evolution of strong deviations from mendelian segregation ratios (meiotic drive).
source: Further, the unique asymmetry of transmission in female meiosis, where only one parental chromosome is transmitted, presents an opportunity for the evolution of strong deviations from mendelian segregation ratios (meiotic drive) (Pardo-Manuel de Villena and Sapienza, 2001; Chmátal et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pardo-Manuel de Villena and Sapienza, 2001 and Chmátal et al., 2014

claim: Recurrent meiotic drive is a potential cause of the evolutionarily rapid divergence of satellite DNAs and centromeric chromatin proteins.
source: Recurrent meiotic drive is a potential cause of the evolutionarily rapid divergence of satellite DNAs and centromeric chromatin proteins (Malik and Henikoff, 2001; Talbert et al., 2004; Rudd et al., 2006; Malik and Henikoff, 2009), as well as the observed high levels of meiotic aneuploidy arising from the tradeoff between fidelity and drive (Zwick et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Malik and Henikoff, 2001; Talbert et al., 2004; Rudd et al., 2006; Malik and Henikoff, 2009

claim: Recurrent meiotic drive is a potential cause of the observed high levels of meiotic aneuploidy arising from the tradeoff between fidelity and drive.
source: Recurrent meiotic drive is a potential cause of the evolutionarily rapid divergence of satellite DNAs and centromeric chromatin proteins (Malik and Henikoff, 2001; Talbert et al., 2004; Rudd et al., 2006; Malik and Henikoff, 2009), as well as the observed high levels of meiotic aneuploidy arising from the tradeoff between fidelity and drive (Zwick et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zwick et al., 1999

claim: Low rates of meiotic exchange in centromere proximal regions might result in large haplotypes in populations, perhaps even spanning the α-satellite arrays.
source: Recognizing the potential research value of well-genotyped diversity across human CPRs, we hypothesized that the low rates of meiotic exchange in these regions (Nambiar and Smith, 2016) might result in large haplotypes in populations, perhaps even spanning the α-satellite arrays.
evidence: Hypothesis based on citation to Nambiar and Smith, 2016 about low recombination rates

claim: UPGMA clustering on 800 SNPs immediately flanking the chrX centromeric gap in males reveals a clear haplotypic structure that spans the gap and extends to approximately 7 Mbp.
source: Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic Mean (UMPGA) clustering on 800 SNPs immediately flanking the chrX centromeric gap in males (Figure 1c) reveals a clear haplotypic structure that spans the gap and extends, as predicted, to a much larger region (≈7 Mbp, Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1b and 1c

claim: Clustering of the imputed genotypes of females falls into the same distinct high-level haplotypes as males.
source: Similar clustering of the imputed genotypes of females also falls into the same distinct high-level haplotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Haplotypes spanning CPRs (cenhaps) exist on chrX and most metacentric chromosomes.
source: This discovery of the predicted haplotypes spanning CPRs (hereafter referred to as cenhaps) on chrX and most metacentric chromosomes (Figure 2) opens a new window into their evolutionary history and functional associations.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: The pattern of geographic differentiation across the inferred chrX CPR exhibits higher diversity in African samples.
source: The pattern of geographic differentiation across the inferred chrX CPR (Figure 1b,c) exhibits higher diversity in African samples, as observed throughout the genome (Auton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1b,c and citation to Auton et al., 2015

claim: A distinctly diverged chrX cenhap (cenhap 1) is fairly common among Africans today but rare outside of Africa.
source: Despite being fairly common among Africans today, a distinctly diverged chrX cenhap (cenhap 1, highlighted in purple, Figure 1b,c) is rare outside of Africa.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1b,c

claim: The estimated Time of the Most Recent Common Ancestor (TMRCA) for the three major chrX cenhaps is approximately 600 KYA.
source: Examination of the haplotypic clustering and estimated synonymous divergence in the coding regions of 21 genes included in the chrX cenhap region (see Figure 1—source data 1) yields a parallel relationship among the three major cenhaps and an estimated Time of the Most Recent Common Ancestor (TMRCA) of ≈600 KYA (Figure 1d) for this most diverged example.
evidence: Supported by analysis of synonymous divergence data shown in Figure 1d

claim: Ancient segments have been inferred in African genomes.
source: While ancient segments have been inferred in African genomes (Hammer et al., 2011; Hsieh et al., 2016), this cenhap stands out as genomically (if not genetically) large.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammer et al., 2011 and Hsieh et al., 2016

claim: The presence of polymorphic ancient cenhaps is inconsistent with the predicted hitchhiking effect of sequential fixation of new meiotically driven centromeres.
source: The presence of such polymorphic ancient cenhaps is inconsistent with the predicted hitchhiking effect of sequential fixation of new meiotically driven centromeres (Malik and Henikoff, 2001).
evidence: Inference based on data and citation to Malik and Henikoff, 2001

claim: The detection of near-ancient segments spanning the centromere contrasts with the observation of substantially more recent ancestry across the remainder of chrX.
source: Further, the detection of near-ancient segments spanning the centromere contrasts with the observation of substantially more recent ancestry across the remainder of chrX and with the expectation of reduced archaic sequences on chrX (Dutheil et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on data and citation to Dutheil et al., 2015

claim: The detection of near-ancient segments spanning the centromere contrasts with the expectation of reduced archaic sequences on chrX.
source: Further, the detection of near-ancient segments spanning the centromere contrasts with the observation of substantially more recent ancestry across the remainder of chrX and with the expectation of reduced archaic sequences on chrX (Dutheil et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on data and citation to Dutheil et al., 2015

claim: Putatively introgressed archaic segments in African genomes have been inferred from genome-wide demographic modeling.
source: Although putatively introgressed archaic segments in African genomes have been inferred from genome-wide demographic modeling (Hammer et al., 2011; Hsieh et al., 2016; Durvasula and Sankararaman, 2019; Speidel et al., 2019), ancient cenhaps could also persist within the ancestral population due to natural selection.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammer et al., 2011; Hsieh et al., 2016; Durvasula and Sankararaman, 2019; Speidel et al., 2019

claim: Ancient cenhaps could persist within the ancestral population due to natural selection.
source: Although putatively introgressed archaic segments in African genomes have been inferred from genome-wide demographic modeling (Hammer et al., 2011; Hsieh et al., 2016; Durvasula and Sankararaman, 2019; Speidel et al., 2019), ancient cenhaps could also persist within the ancestral population due to natural selection.
evidence: Speculative alternative explanation for ancient cenhaps

claim: Studies firmly establish genome-wide evidence of recent introgression into Eurasian populations of anatomically modern humans.
source: Such studies firmly establish genome-wide evidence of recent introgression into Eurasian populations of AMHs (Green et al., 2010; Patterson et al., 2012; Sankararaman et al., 2012; Prüfer et al., 2014; Sankararaman et al., 2014; Prüfer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 2010; Patterson et al., 2012; Sankararaman et al., 2012; Prüfer et al., 2014; Sankararaman et al., 2014; Prüfer et al., 2017

claim: The most diverged chr11 cenhap lineage (cenhap 1) contains a small basal group of primarily out-of-Africa genomes.
source: The most diverged lineage contains a small basal group of primarily out-of-Africa genomes (cenhap 1, highlighted in green).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Chr11 cenhap 1 carries a large proportion of the derived alleles assigned to the Neanderthal lineage, with DM/(DM+DN)=0.98.
source: This cenhap carries a large proportion of the derived alleles assigned to the Neanderthal lineage, DM/(DM+DN)=0.98, where DM is the cenhap mean number of shared Neanderthal Derived Matches and DN is the cenhap mean number of Neanderthal Derived Non-matches (Figure 3a, at left).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Chr11 cenhap 1 has a ratio DM/(DM+AN)=0.91, suggesting that this large cenhap lineage, including the centromere and satellite sequences, shared most of its evolutionary history with Neanderthals.
source: The ratio DM/(DM+AN)=0.91, where AN is the number of Neanderthal-cenhap Non-matches that are Ancestral in the Neanderthal, suggests that this large cenhap lineage, including the centromere and satellite sequences, shared most of its evolutionary history with Neanderthals.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: The diverged chr11 cenhap 1 is limited to populations outside of Africa, supporting the conclusion that it is an introgressed archaic centromere.
source: This diverged cenhap is limited to populations outside of Africa, supporting the conclusion that it is an introgressed archaic centromere.
evidence: Inference based on geographic distribution data

claim: The affinity of chr11 cenhap 1 to Neanderthals is slightly stronger than to Denisovans.
source: Figure 3b shows these mean counts for each SNP class by cenhap group, confirming that the affinity to Neanderthals is slightly stronger than to Denisovans.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3b

claim: A second basal chr11 lineage (cenhap 2) found principally in Africa separates shortly after the inferred Neanderthal.
source: A second basal lineage found principally in Africa (cenhap 2, highlighted in purple, Figure 3a) separates shortly after the inferred Neanderthal.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3a

claim: It is unclear if chr11 cenhap 2 represents an introgression from a distinct archaic hominin in Africa or a surviving ancient lineage within the population that gave rise to anatomically modern humans.
source: It is unclear if this cenhap represents an introgression from a distinct archaic hominin in Africa or a surviving ancient lineage within the population that gave rise to AMHs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of data

claim: The CPRs of other chromosomes include diverged, basal lineages that are likely to be relatively old, if not archaic.
source: Notably, the CPRs of other chromosomes include diverged, basal lineages that are likely to be relatively old, if not archaic (Figure 2).
evidence: Inference based on data shown in Figure 2

claim: Chromosome 8 contains an ancient cenhap limited to Africa with an estimated TMRCA of approximately 730 KYA.
source: Two examples are chromosome 8, containing an ancient cenhap limited to Africa with an estimated TMRCA of ~730 KYA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and chr10 that appears to harbor another clear Neanderthal cenhap introgression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Chr10 appears to harbor another clear Neanderthal cenhap introgression.
source: Two examples are chromosome 8, containing an ancient cenhap limited to Africa with an estimated TMRCA of ~730 KYA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and chr10 that appears to harbor another clear Neanderthal cenhap introgression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The very large genomic sizes of ancient cenhaps could allow identification of archaic homology even with modest genomic sequence coverages from archaic fossils.
source: It should be noted that the very large genomic sizes of these ancient cenhaps could allow identification of archaic homology even with modest genomic sequence coverages from archaic fossils.
evidence: Inference based on the observed large size of cenhaps

claim: The paucity of exchange in centromere proximal regions would create cenhap associations with satellite divergence in both sequence and array size.
source: While the divergence of satellites may be dynamic on a shorter time scale (Smith, 1976), we reasoned that the paucity of exchange in these regions would create cenhap associations with satellite divergence in both sequence and array size.
evidence: Inference based on low recombination and citation to Smith, 1976

claim: Miga et al. (2014) reported a bimodal distribution in estimated chrX-specific α-satellite array (DXZ1) sizes for a subset of the 1000 Genomes males.
source: Miga et al. (2014) generated chromosome-specific graphical models of the α-satellite arrays and reported a bimodal distribution in estimated chrX-specific α-satellite array (DXZ1) sizes (Willard et al., 1983) for a subset of the 1000 Genomes males.
evidence: Supported by citations to Miga et al. (2014) and Willard et al., 1983

claim: The cumulative distributions of estimated array sizes of the three common chrX cenhaps show substantial differences.
source: The cumulative distributions of estimated array sizes of the three common chrX cenhaps designated in Figure 1c show substantial differences (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4a

claim: α-satellite array sizes in cenhap-homozygous females are parallel to males, and imputed cenhap heterozygotes are intermediate, as expected.
source: α-satellite array sizes in cenhap-homozygous females are parallel to males, and imputed cenhap heterozygotes are intermediate, as expected.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: There is variation in array size between cenhap homozygotes on chr11.
source: Similarly, Figure 4b shows an even more striking example of variation in array size between cenhap homozygotes on chr11, and Figure 4c demonstrates that heterozygotes of the two most common cenhaps are reliably intermediate in size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4b

claim: Heterozygotes of the two most common chr11 cenhaps are reliably intermediate in array size.
source: Similarly, Figure 4b shows an even more striking example of variation in array size between cenhap homozygotes on chr11, and Figure 4c demonstrates that heterozygotes of the two most common cenhaps are reliably intermediate in size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4c

claim: Reference bias does not explain the observed cenhaps with large array size on chrX and chr11.
source: While we confirmed that reference bias does not explain the observed cenhaps with large array size on chrX and chr11 (see Materials and methods, Figure 1b, Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), it is a potential explanation for particular instances of cenhaps with small estimated array sizes, for example the relatively low chrX-specific α-satellite content in the highly diverged African cenhap (see Figure 1b,c and Figure 4a, cenhap 1, highlighted in purple).
evidence: Supported by analysis described in Materials and methods and data shown in figures

claim: Reference bias is a potential explanation for particular instances of cenhaps with small estimated array sizes.
source: While we confirmed that reference bias does not explain the observed cenhaps with large array size on chrX and chr11 (see Materials and methods, Figure 1b, Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), it is a potential explanation for particular instances of cenhaps with small estimated array sizes, for example the relatively low chrX-specific α-satellite content in the highly diverged African cenhap (see Figure 1b,c and Figure 4a, cenhap 1, highlighted in purple).
evidence: Speculative explanation for small array sizes

claim: Cenhaps robustly tag a substantial component of the genetic variation in array size.
source: Importantly, our results demonstrate that cenhaps do robustly tag a substantial component of the genetic variation in array size.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: Binding of the centromere-specific histone, CENPA, scales with the size of arrays.
source: Both binding of the centromere-specific histone, CENPA (Sullivan et al., 2011), and kinetochore size (Iwata-Otsubo et al., 2017) are known to scale with the size of arrays and to fluctuate with sequence variation in satellite DNAs (Aldrup-MacDonald et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sullivan et al., 2011

claim: Kinetochore size scales with the size of arrays.
source: Both binding of the centromere-specific histone, CENPA (Sullivan et al., 2011), and kinetochore size (Iwata-Otsubo et al., 2017) are known to scale with the size of arrays and to fluctuate with sequence variation in satellite DNAs (Aldrup-MacDonald et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iwata-Otsubo et al., 2017

claim: CENPA binding and kinetochore size fluctuate with sequence variation in satellite DNAs.
source: Both binding of the centromere-specific histone, CENPA (Sullivan et al., 2011), and kinetochore size (Iwata-Otsubo et al., 2017) are known to scale with the size of arrays and to fluctuate with sequence variation in satellite DNAs (Aldrup-MacDonald et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aldrup-MacDonald et al., 2016

claim: α-satellite array variations can affect mitotic stability in human cells.
source: Through these interactions with kinetochore function and other roles for heterochromatin in chromosome segregation (Dernburg et al., 1996; Karpen et al., 1996; Peng and Karpen, 2008), α-satellite array variations can affect mitotic stability in human cells (Sullivan et al., 2017), as well as meiotic drive systems in the mouse (Chmátal et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dernburg et al., 1996; Karpen et al., 1996; Peng and Karpen, 2008; Sullivan et al., 2017

claim: α-satellite array variations can affect meiotic drive systems in the mouse.
source: Through these interactions with kinetochore function and other roles for heterochromatin in chromosome segregation (Dernburg et al., 1996; Karpen et al., 1996; Peng and Karpen, 2008), α-satellite array variations can affect mitotic stability in human cells (Sullivan et al., 2017), as well as meiotic drive systems in the mouse (Chmátal et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chmátal et al., 2014

claim: Meiotic drive has been proposed as the likely explanation for the saltatory divergence of satellite sequences.
source: Meiotic drive has been proposed as the likely explanation for the saltatory divergence of satellite sequences and the excess of nonsynonymous divergence of several centromere proteins, some of which interact directly with the DNA (Malik and Henikoff, 2001; Talbert et al., 2004; Malik and Henikoff, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Malik and Henikoff, 2001; Talbert et al., 2004; Malik and Henikoff, 2009

claim: Meiotic drive has been proposed as the likely explanation for the excess of nonsynonymous divergence of several centromere proteins.
source: Meiotic drive has been proposed as the likely explanation for the saltatory divergence of satellite sequences and the excess of nonsynonymous divergence of several centromere proteins, some of which interact directly with the DNA (Malik and Henikoff, 2001; Talbert et al., 2004; Malik and Henikoff, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Malik and Henikoff, 2001; Talbert et al., 2004; Malik and Henikoff, 2009

claim: The high levels of haplotypic diversity and deep cenhap lineages observed conflict with the predictions of a naïve turnover model based on recurrent strong directional selection yielding sequential fixation of new centromeric haplotypes.
source: However, the high levels of haplotypic diversity and deep cenhap lineages observed (Figure 2) conflict with the predictions of a naïve turnover model based on recurrent strong directional selection yielding sequential fixation of new centromeric haplotypes.
evidence: Inference based on data shown in Figure 2

claim: The levels of synonymous diversity in the few coding genes in the CPR of chrX are 0.00062 (0.00043–0.00128).
source: Indeed, the levels of synonymous diversity, πs, in the few coding genes in the CPR of chrX, 0.00062 (0.00043–0.00128) and chr11, 0.00128 (0.00088–0.00217), are not different from levels of diversity in non-CPR regions (Dutheil et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: The levels of synonymous diversity in the few coding genes in the CPR of chr11 are 0.00128 (0.00088–0.00217).
source: Indeed, the levels of synonymous diversity, πs, in the few coding genes in the CPR of chrX, 0.00062 (0.00043–0.00128) and chr11, 0.00128 (0.00088–0.00217), are not different from levels of diversity in non-CPR regions (Dutheil et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: The levels of synonymous diversity in CPR genes are not different from levels of diversity in non-CPR regions.
source: Indeed, the levels of synonymous diversity, πs, in the few coding genes in the CPR of chrX, 0.00062 (0.00043–0.00128) and chr11, 0.00128 (0.00088–0.00217), are not different from levels of diversity in non-CPR regions (Dutheil et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on data analysis and citation to Dutheil et al., 2015

claim: The genes in the CPR of chr8 show a considerably lower mean synonymous diversity of 0.00010 (0.00007–0.00019).
source: The genes in the CPR of chr8 show a considerably lower mean πs, 0.00010 (0.00007–0.00019); but we note there are only eight genes and their mean divergence from Pan orthologs is also low (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3—source data 2

claim: Among the 37 genes in the chr11 CPR are 34 of the approximately 300 known odorant receptors (ORs).
source: Among the 37 genes in the chr11 CPR are 34 of the ~300 known (Malnic et al., 2004) odorant receptors (ORs).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and citation to Malnic et al., 2004

claim: Nonsynonymous SNPs in chr11 ORs are associated with variation in human olfactory perception of particular volatile chemicals.
source: Nonsynonymous SNPs in these chr11 ORs are associated with variation in human olfactory perception of particular volatile chemicals (Trimmer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trimmer et al., 2019

claim: 73 amino acid replacement polymorphisms are observed in 25 of the chr11 ORs.
source: 73 amino acid replacements polymorphisms are observed in 25 of these ORs (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—source data 1

claim: The vast majority (63) of amino acid replacement polymorphisms in chr11 ORs are on the lineages to the two putative archaic cenhaps.
source: The vast majority (63) are on the lineages to the two putative archaic cenhaps.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: 60 amino acid replacement polymorphisms in chr11 ORs are on the lineage to the Neanderthal haplotype, suggesting this cenhap encodes Neanderthal-specific determinants of smell and taste.
source: Indeed, 60 are on the lineage to the Neanderthal haplotype suggesting this cenhap encodes Neanderthal-specific determinants of smell and taste.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: In the second putative archaic African chr11 cenhap, seven ORs harbor ten amino acid replacements, of which only one is shared with cenhap 1.
source: Similarly, in the second putative archaic African cenhap, seven of these ORs harbor ten amino acid replacements, of which only one is shared with cenhap 1 (see Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—source data 1

claim: The frequencies of the Neanderthal chr11 cenhap in Europe, South Asia and the Americas are 0.061, 0.032 and 0.033 respectively.
source: The frequencies of the Neanderthal cenhap in Europe, South Asia and the Americas (0.061, 0.032 and 0.033 respectively), and of second ancient cenhap in Africa (0.036), are sufficiently high that together they contribute ≈ 18% of the amino acid replacement diversity in these 34 ORs among the 1000 Genomes.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: The frequency of the second ancient chr11 cenhap in Africa is 0.036.
source: The frequencies of the Neanderthal cenhap in Europe, South Asia and the Americas (0.061, 0.032 and 0.033 respectively), and of second ancient cenhap in Africa (0.036), are sufficiently high that together they contribute ≈ 18% of the amino acid replacement diversity in these 34 ORs among the 1000 Genomes.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: The two ancient chr11 cenhaps together contribute approximately 18% of the amino acid replacement diversity in 34 ORs among the 1000 Genomes.
source: The frequencies of the Neanderthal cenhap in Europe, South Asia and the Americas (0.061, 0.032 and 0.033 respectively), and of second ancient cenhap in Africa (0.036), are sufficiently high that together they contribute ≈ 18% of the amino acid replacement diversity in these 34 ORs among the 1000 Genomes.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: A substantial and rather unique part of the variation in chemical perception among anatomically modern humans may be contributed by the two ancient chr11 cenhaps.
source: Thus, a substantial and rather unique part of the variation in chemical perception among AMH may be contributed by these two ancient cenhaps.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: The most diverged, basal clade in the chr12 CPR is common in Africa but not represented among the descendants of the out-of-Africa migrations.
source: The most diverged, basal clade in the chr12 CPR (Figure 3c, indicated in brown) is common in Africa, but, like the most diverged chrX cenhap, is not represented among the descendants of the out-of-Africa migrations (Bae et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3c and citation to Bae et al., 2017

claim: Members of the basal chr12 cenhap share fewer matches with derived SNPs on the Neanderthal and Denisovan lineages (DM) and exhibit strikingly more ancestral non-matches (AN) than other chr12 cenhaps.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that this branch split off before that of Neanderthals/Denisovans, members of this cenhap share fewer matches with derived SNPs on the Neanderthal and Denisovan lineages (DM) and exhibit strikingly more ancestral non-matches (AN) than other chr12 cenhaps (see Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3b

claim: The putatively archaic chr12 cenhap represents a large and obvious example of the potentially introgressed sequences within African populations inferred from model-based analyses of the distributions of sequence divergence.
source: This putatively archaic chr12 cenhap represents a large and obvious example of the potentially introgressed sequences within African populations inferred from model-based analyses of the distributions of sequence divergence (Hammer et al., 2011; Hsieh et al., 2016; Durvasula and Sankararaman, 2019).
evidence: Inference based on data and citations to Hammer et al., 2011; Hsieh et al., 2016; Durvasula and Sankararaman, 2019

claim: A small out-of-Africa chr12 cenhap nested within a mostly African subclade appears to be a typical Eurasian archaic introgression with higher affinity to Neanderthals (DM/(DN + DM)=0.91 and DM/(DM +AN)=0.90) than to Denisovans.
source: The small out-of-Africa cenhap nested within a mostly African subclade (indicated in blue in Figure 3c) appears to be a typical Eurasian archaic introgression with higher affinity to Neanderthals (DM/(DN + DM)=0.91 and DM/(DM +AN)=0.90) than to Denisovans (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3b and 3c

claim: The basal chr12 cenhap is twice as diverged as the apparent introgressed Neanderthal cenhap, placing the TMRCA at approximately 1.1 MYA, assuming the Neanderthal TMRCA was 575KYA.
source: Based on the numbers of SNPs underlying the cenhaps, this basal cenhap is twice as diverged as the apparent introgressed Neanderthal cenhap, placing the TMRCA at ~1.1 MYA, assuming the Neanderthal TMRCA was 575KYA (Prüfer et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on data analysis and citation to Prüfer et al., 2017

claim: The large genomic scale of the most diverged chr12 cenhap (relative to apparent exchanges in other cenhaps) is consistent with recent admixture with an extinct archaic in Africa.
source: While there is no direct evidence of recent introgression, the large genomic scale of the most diverged chr12 cenhap (relative to apparent exchanges in other cenhaps) is consistent with recent admixture with an extinct archaic in Africa; yet, again, selective maintenance of ancient cenhaps with associated suppression of crossing over is an alternative explanation.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: Selective maintenance of ancient cenhaps with associated suppression of crossing over is an alternative explanation for the large genomic scale of the most diverged chr12 cenhap.
source: While there is no direct evidence of recent introgression, the large genomic scale of the most diverged chr12 cenhap (relative to apparent exchanges in other cenhaps) is consistent with recent admixture with an extinct archaic in Africa; yet, again, selective maintenance of ancient cenhaps with associated suppression of crossing over is an alternative explanation.
evidence: Speculative alternative explanation

claim: Cenhaps can be investigated for associations with variation in meiotic drive.
source: Most importantly, cenhaps can now be investigated for associations with variation in evolutionarily important chromosome functions, such as meiotic drive (Meyer et al., 2012) and recombination (Nambiar and Smith, 2016), as well as disease-related functions, such as aneuploidy in the germline (Nagaoka et al., 2012) and in development (McCoy, 2017), cancer and aging (Naylor and van Deursen, 2016).
